stories.headline: Messi scores but Nashville strikes late to deny Miami win
stories.summary: Lionel Messi scored a second-half goal but Nashville SC struck back in stoppage time to earn a 2-2 draw at Inter Miami and maintain its nine-point lead at the top of the Eastern Conference.
stories.body:
Lionel Messi scored a second-half goal but Nashville SC struck back in stoppage time to earn a 2-2 draw at Inter Miami and maintain its nine-point lead at the top of the Eastern Conference.

Messi looked to have given Miami the win when he exchanged passes with longtime Argentina teammate Rodrigo De Paul before picking out the side of the net with a precise left-footed finish from 20 yards out in 62nd minute.

Twice Messi came close to extending Miami's lead and scoring what would have been his 100th for the MLS club in all competitions. But he was denied first by a Brian Schwake save onto the post and then by a last-ditch headed clearance by Nashville defender Jeisson Palacios.

Miami was then hit by a sucker punch in the first minute of added time when Sam Surridge fired Nashville level. Surridge had earlier put Nashville in front after just four minutes in South Florida.

Miami has now dropped 11 points from winning positions at home in MLS this season, second only behind New York City FC and CF Montréal.

Saturday's dropped points could prove particularly costly, leaving Miami trailing Nashville by nine points in the battle for both the Eastern Conference's No. 1 seed and the Supporters' Shield with nine game remaining.

Nashville, which joined MLS as an expansion team alongside Miami in 2020, is now in prime position to claim its first Supporters' Shield.

Miami, which is still awaiting Cristian 'Kily' González to formerly take over as coach, has won just once in its last nine games in all competitions.

The team, and Messi, had plenty of chances to add to that win total on Saturday.

Messi had a big hand in bringing Miami level in the 19th minute, when his inswinging corner forced an own goal after it deflected into the net off the head of Nashville defender Reed Baker-Whiting.

Messi then had a shot blocked from outside the box in the 27th minute and sent a free kick wide shortly afterward before breaking through in the second half with his MLS-leading 19th goal of the season.

But the 39-year-old couldn't add to that total as he hit the crossbar as well as the post in the second half. Even after Nashville leveled in added time, De Paul was inches away from giving Miami the win when his shot hit the outside of the post.

Nashville is now unbeaten in four matches against Miami this season. As well as a 4-1 win the teams' previous MLS meeting on Aug. 15, Nashville also eliminated Miami from the Concacaf Champions Cup earlier this season.

Information from ESPN Research and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

stories.headline: Brewers pour it on early as Garrett Mitchell leads the way in 13-9 victory over the Reds
stories.summary: — Garrett Mitchell went 4 for 5 with a homer and four RBI as the Milwaukee Brewers scored all their runs in the first five innings of a 13-9 victory over the Cincinnati Reds on Saturday night.
stories.body:
MILWAUKEE -- — Garrett Mitchell went 4 for 5 with a homer and four RBI as the Milwaukee Brewers scored all their runs in the first five innings of a 13-9 victory over the Cincinnati Reds on Saturday night.


William Contreras hit a tiebreaking three-run homer in the fourth inning and Brice Turang added a two-run shot one night after the Brewers clinched a playoff berth by trouncing the Reds 20-0. Never before in franchise history had the Brewers totaled that many runs in a two-game stretch.


The Reds headed to Milwaukee after losing 14-1 to the Los Angeles Dodgers on Wednesday, so they’ve allowed 47 runs over their last three games. According to Sportradar, the last time the Reds gave up 47-plus runs over a three-game stretch was in September 1901.


No major league team has given up that many runs in a span of three games since July 2022, when the Boston Red Sox allowed 55.


The Brewers’ magic number for clinching the NL Central dropped to three.


Eugenio Suárez and Juan Brito homered for Cincinnati.


Turang and Mitchell hit two-run homers off Brady Singer (6-14) in the first inning to give Milwaukee a 4-0 lead. Cincinnati rallied off Shane Drohan to tie it at 5-all on Brito’s two-run blast in the fourth.


Milwaukee responded with three runs in the fourth and five in the fifth.


Singer allowed eight runs in four innings. Graham Ashcraft allowed five runs in the fifth while retiring only one batter.


Chad Patrick (9-4) got the win by striking out four in 1 1/3 innings of scoreless relief. Abner Uribe worked the ninth for his seventh save.


The news wasn’t all good for the Brewers.


In his first relief appearance of the season, Kyle Harrison allowed hits to each of the four batters he faced, and they all ended up scoring. Harrison has given up 19 runs – 17 earned – over 7 1/3 innings in his last three outings as his ERA has climbed from 2.79 to 3.98.


Up next
Chase Burns (15-3, 2.73 ERA) pitches for the Reds on Sunday. The Brewers haven't announced their starter.

stories.headline: 2026 FIBA Women's World Cup: USA-France gold medal game preview
stories.summary: It's the World Cup finale fans wanted to see: USA and France will meet in a rematch of the Olympic gold medal game.
stories.body:
It's the matchup everyone has been waiting to see.

The U.S. women's basketball team's mastery of international play was tested two years ago in Paris, during a one-point win over France in the Olympic final. In Sunday's FIBA Women's World Cup gold medal match (2 p.m. ET), the French hope to get their revenge.

Team USA beat Spain 76-66 on Saturday after France defeated host Germany 86-64 in Berlin. That leaves the top two teams to meet in the final. Since 1996, the United States has won every Olympic and World Cup gold except one: in the 2006 World Cup, when the Americans lost to Russia in the semifinals and took bronze.

France has been building as a national power, with 13 French players in the WNBA this season, including the Golden State Valkyries' Gabby Williams, who has dual citizenship and is a crucial player for Team France. She had 22 points and five rebounds Saturday.

The U.S. women had a slow start Saturday and led 39-36 at halftime. The score was tied 58-58 after three quarters. But Team USA took control in the fourth quarter, outscoring Spain 18-8. New York Liberty forward Breanna Stewart had 16 points to lead the Americans, who had a big edge at the free throw line, going 27-of-35 to Spain's 10-of-11.

Can Team USA finish the job for its fifth consecutive and 12th overall World Cup gold medal? Or will France win its first? Here's how they match up and how each could win.

How France advanced

Voepel: Williams led four French players who scored in double figures and was also a big part of the defensive effort that forced Germany into 25 turnovers. That was the key stat, as France had just six turnovers.

Germany trailed 25-23 after the first quarter. But France built its lead to seven at halftime and with so many turnovers, Germany couldn't build a sustained comeback effort in the second half.

Williams' Golden State teammate Janelle Salaun had 14 points and 11 rebounds. Liberty's Marine Johannes had 13 points, and the Phoenix Mercury's Valeriane Ayayi had 10. The French were outrebounded 41-31, but their huge turnover advantage overrode that.

The French have won their five World Cup games by an average of 35.6 points, with Saturday's 22-point margin the closest.

Philippou: I can't overstate how good France has looked this tournament. Though their group was not particularly strong, in the knockout rounds the French crushed China and mostly had their way against Germany. They've had the best offense in Berlin, scoring 96.2 points per game, shooting 51.6% from the field and converting 44.2% of their shots from the 3-point arc -- hence Stewart's postgame comment that they are "shooting the s--- out of the ball." Those are numbers we are used to seeing from Team USA! And of course, France's defensive identity is its foundation. Williams has been exceptional this tournament and looks determined to will her team to a historic gold on Sunday.

How the USA advanced

Voepel: As was the case in Team USA's tight 55-52 victory over Italy in group play, the veterans took over to close out the win over Spain. Along with Stewart, the Mercury's Kahleah Copper (13 points) and the Las Vegas Aces' Jackie Young (12) scored in double figures.

The USA reserves did contribute, though, with how they helped the Americans catch up after Spain's hot start. The Indiana Fever's Aliyah Boston and Dallas Wings' Paige Bueckers led the bench with 6 points each.

But with tensions high in a tie game going into the fourth quarter, the Americans relied on their players who have the most international experience to stay calm and make key plays at crunch time. Team USA had 15 turnovers in the game, but only one in the final quarter.

The Americans shot 40% from the field (23 of 58) and just 17% (3 of 18) from behind the arc. But their advantage at the line and their ability to hold Spain to 38% from the field (25 of 66) was enough to pull out the victory.

Philippou: That fourth quarter was finally when the U.S. women could find a semblance of rhythm, and it isn't a coincidence that was when they played their best defense of the game, holding Spain to just eight points. The execution on that end seemed to carry over offensively.

U.S. coach Kara Lawson primarily leaned on her vets late, though she gave Caitlin Clark a good run in that frame and Boston played all 10 minutes.

"We had certain things we wanted to attack, and I thought we got to those in the fourth to score," Lawson said. "I thought defensively it was the best we had played from guarding the ball to guarding the ball screen to boxing out and limiting to one shot. Just every phase of defense, we were precise and we were locked in.

"And so when we get all that going together, then we feel like we can create some separation. But our execution late, our shot making late, our understanding of mismatches late was all at a high level."

How do France-USA match up? What can we take away from the Olympic meeting?

Voepel: The French have not had a close game in this World Cup while the Americans have had two. Just based on how each team's five games in Berlin have played out so far, France has looked better. A possible advantage for the U.S. women is that they've had to dig deep and execute in crucial moments during their wins over Italy and Spain. So perhaps that will help in what's expected to be a close matchup with the French.

It has seemed like Team USA's offense has been feast (94 points vs. China, 105 vs. Czechia and 108 vs. Hungary), famine (55 vs. Italy) or frustrating (76 points vs. Spain, with USA taking too many bad shots and missing too many good ones). But the U.S. women are still where they expected to be against the foe they expected to face. Now which Team USA offense will show up Sunday?

Looking back on the 2024 gold medal game in Paris, the Las Vegas Aces' A'ja Wilson -- who is dealing with a back issue and isn't playing in the World Cup -- led the Americans with 21 points and 13 rebounds. Copper and Kelsey Plum (also out of this tournament with a leg injury) had 12 points in that game.

Williams led France with 19 points, 7 rebounds and 3 steals -- and almost sent the game to overtime. She made a shot at the buzzer, but her foot was touching the 3-point line. That was the difference between playing an extra period for gold in Paris and leaving with a silver. It kept alive the United States' streak of eight consecutive Olympic gold medals.

Philippou: Lawson has said the sign of a good team is one that can win even when it's not making the shots it normally does. Still, USA's offense at best hasn't been consistent this tournament, and it feels more than likely Sunday could be another tough day for the unit against Les Bleues' defensive pressure.

"[The French] have great depth, they have great athleticism, and they found their style," said Olaf Lange, German national team coach and current associate head coach for the Toronto Tempo. "They're pretty much trying to jump every team with their pressure. ... We know from the Paris Olympics that this is also not easy to handle for USA. They probably have the tools, but they have way less chemistry than most international or European nations."

What could be Sunday's X factor?

Philippou: I'm fascinated to see how the psychological element of a game like this plays out and to observe how pressure impacts both team. Marine Johannes said that France feels like it has nothing to lose, but I'm not sure I buy that. There's clearly a desire to avenge the Olympic loss, and even some pressure to finally get French basketball on top.

"All we care about is winning," Dom Malonga said after the quarterfinal. "The French national team has been known for years for like second place or semifinals, never all the way, even in EuroBasket, until now -- I feel like we have to do it. We have to make it happen."

France also doesn't have as much experience in these moments as the United States. At the same time, USA has six players who haven't played at the World Cup or Olympics in any capacity. And yet the pressure all 12 of those players carry is to not be the team that essentially screws up -- all while, as Stewart noted, keeping emotions in check.

"[The pressure] is constant," Stewart told ESPN. "Team USA, we haven't lost a World Cup game since '06. The same with the Olympics, however many gold medals in a row. It's not bad pressure. It's just the standard of what we do here. But it's like, we have to know what we're protecting and know what we're chasing.

"You can't shy away from it. You just have to embrace it. Like, this is the standard. This is the standard that those before me put into place, and now we make it the standard, and we just continue to keep it."

Voepel: The Americans could help themselves if they can hit more 3-point shots. They struggled there Saturday, and it impacted their offensive effectiveness. The United States made 12 3-pointers vs. China and Hungary, one vs. Italy, seven vs. Czechia and three against Spain.

By contrast, France has been much better from behind the arc, making at least 10 3-pointers in every game with a high of 22 (on 40 shots) in its 111-56 win over Nigeria on Monday. The Americans will need to try to slow down France from long range while also shooting better themselves.

stories.summary: The NFL is back, and so are the uniform combinations. Here's a look at what each team is wearing in Week 1.
stories.body:
Week 1 of the NFL season always marks one of the best times of the year. Renewed optimism brings positive feelings and vibes around one's favorite team. But the uniforms always seem to be a little crisper, too. This year is no different.

It's never too early to wear a throwback look, and the Minnesota Vikings will do exactly that in Week 1. Minnesota is rocking "The Vikings Classic" against the Green Bay Packers at home Sunday. The uniforms first debuted in Week 1 of 2023 and include a deeper hue of purple, paying homage to the team's "earlier voyages." The numbers are larger than normal and include a gold trim.

Meanwhile, the Cincinnati Bengals are wearing orange threads for their "Open In Orange" theme against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. The Carolina Panthers will ring in the new season with black helmets against the Chicago Bears.

The season kicks off when the Seattle Seahawks host the New England Patriots on Wednesday night. It's a traditional look for both sides, with Seattle rocking all-college navy and the Patriots wearing white jerseys with navy pants, slightly different than their Super Bowl LX matchup in February.

stories.headline: Fenerbahce coach returns to work after resignation confusion
stories.summary: Fenerbahce coach Ismail Kartal returned to his duties on Saturday, contradicting media reports from the day before suggesting his resignation was final.
stories.body:
ISTANBUL -- Fenerbahce coach Ismail Kartal returned to his duties on Saturday, contradicting media reports from the day before suggesting his resignation was final.

Kartal had announced he was quitting his role following Thursday's draw against AS Roma in the Champions League but the club refused to accept his resignation.

Kartal, nevertheless, failed to attend training on Friday ahead of a Superlig game against Gaziantep FK.

However, Fenerbahce released a statement late Friday saying Kartal would resume his duties on Saturday for the Super Lig match against Gaziantep on Monday.

On Saturday, the club's official X account showed photos of him at work.

Kartal had resigned to the surprise of the club and its players in his news conference following the 1-1 draw with Roma to begin the Turkish club's Champions League season.

"First of all, I congratulate my players for carrying out the tasks I assigned for tonight's match to the letter. We played football worthy of the Champions League," the state-run Anadolu Agency quoted Kartal as saying on Thursday. "We could have won the match; we had clear chances. The match ended in a draw, and I am proud of my players."

Kartal continued: "Tonight, I am resigning from my position -- never to return. I extend my heartfelt thanks to my players."

In a separate news conference soon after, club chairman Aziz Yildirim said Fenerbahce fans had hurled a water bottle at Kartal, describing the incident as a reason for the coach's decision. Kartal was also upset by a series of social media posts, Yildirim said.

Yildirim insisted that Kartal's resignation was not accepted and that he would remain at the helm.

"You saw the state Ismail was in. Can a person endure that much distress?" Yildirim said. "They threw a water bottle at Ismail Kartal's head. We saw it. That is why he is upset."

"Ismail Kartal remains in his post," Yildirim added. "I said [to Kartal]: 'You will continue,' and that was that."

Despite reports in Turkey that Fenerbahce official Oguz Cetin later met with Kartal but failed to convince him to stay, Kartal is now set to take charge of the team's fixture against Gaziantep FK on Monday.

Fenerbahce is 11th in the 18-team league.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

stories.headline: Max Verstappen says F1 should consult drivers on new circuits amid Spanish Grand Prix concerns
stories.summary: Max Verstappen has called on Formula 1 to consult drivers when designing new circuits amid concerns there will be no overtaking at Sunday's inaugural race at the all-new Madring.
stories.body:
MADRID -- Max Verstappen has called on Formula 1 to consult drivers when designing new circuits amid concerns there will be no overtaking at Sunday's inaugural race at the all-new Madring.

This year the Spanish Grand Prix has moved to Madrid on a new hybrid street circuit featuring 22 corners and multiple high-speed sections.

Verstappen qualified his Red Bull third on the grid -- behind Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli and McLaren's Lando Norris on pole position -- but doubts there will be any opportunities to move up the order after the start.

"It will be tough, I mean, let's say best case scenario and you're faster [than the car in front], you still can't pass," he said.

"There are no corners where you can pass, so you need to rely on people degging [suffering tyre degradation] very aggressively. So yeah, it's going to be tough.

"I mean, in the long runs it was very tough with a lot of deg for everyone, so that will be probably the key point tomorrow. But even with that, I need to still figure out a corner where you can pass."

Turn 5 has been highlighted as the best overtaking opportunity, but the curved braking zone on the approach to the slow-speed chicane means the lead driver can easily defend by positioning their car in the middle of the track.

What's more, Verstappen said the combination of braking and turning in an F1 car makes the challenge of overtaking even more difficult.

"The corners, like I said before, you can't overtake," he added. "So, in some places, the braking zones, they need to learn that it should never be that you have to steer and combine with the braking because it doesn't allow any kind of overtaking. So, for sure, in terms of track design, I think it can be better."

- McLaren's Lando Norris pips Kimi Antonelli to take thrilling pole for Spanish Grand Prix

- Will Madring live up to reputation as F1 car killer? 'The most risky circuit of the calendar'

- Carlos Sainz hit with three-place grid penalty for home Spanish Grand Prix

Verstappen questioned why F1 track designers do not consult current drivers on circuit designs, saying there are always ways to promote overtaking on a completely new layout.

"I think also input from drivers in the future on track design can also help a lot," the four-time champion said.

"I know they will always come back to you and say 'yeah, but the space [is not available].' Yes, but there's always a way to find an overtaking opportunity around a track.

"But, overall, the event itself is very cool. I mean, yes, they've done a great job. Also, how quickly they made the track available, the information that was shared for the simulator. So, in that sense, I think it was very good.

"But, in terms of if you want to have better racing, overtaking, I think there can be a few corners that can be changed."

Verstappen also said the circuit's signature corner -- the banked La Monumental -- had not lived up to expectations in qualifying due to the need to preserve battery energy for later in the lap.

The Red Bull driver has been one of the biggest critics of F1's new engine formula for 2026, which requires nearly 50% of peak power to be derived from the car's battery pack.

Verstappen said he had looked forward to the corner prior to arriving in Madrid, but was unable to take it flat out for fear of draining the battery.

"Well, I wanted to go flat, but then my battery died," he said. "I had to add a lift, to have better deployment [of energy further around the lap].

"So that's my La Monumental experience.

"Yeah, I mean, it's cool, the banking, but I think they should have done it the other way around, though -- initially more banking and then just flatten it out.

"But in an F1 car you have so much downforce. I think it's more challenging in the other categories [Formula 2 and Formula 3] because it didn't look so easy flat in other categories.

"For us, plus because our battery dies towards the end, so you already slow down a bit. But, I mean, I guess for the shots it looks great from the outside."

stories.headline: Golden Knights extend Mark Stone with 2-year, $18M deal
stories.summary: Golden Knights captain Mark Stone has signed a two-year contract extension with a $9 million annual value that goes through the 2028-29 season.
stories.body:
LAS VEGAS -- Golden Knights captain Mark Stone signed a two-year contract extension Saturday with a $9 million annual value that goes through the 2028-29 season.

He will make $9.5 million this season in the final year of his current deal.

Stone, 34, is coming off a season in which he totaled a career-high 73 points (28 goals, 45 assists) for a Golden Knights team that advanced to the Stanley Cup Final before losing to the Carolina Hurricanes in six games.

Known for boisterous goal celebrations, Stone is the emotional driver behind the Golden Knights, having played in 400 career games for the club. He also has produced, scoring 136 goals with 260 assists and a +112 rating.

Stone has 259 goals and 448 assists over a 15-year career, including more than six seasons with Ottawa before his trade to Vegas on Feb. 25, 2019.

Injuries have kept Stone from delivering even more, but he has played in at least 60 games each of the past two seasons. If Stone can stay healthy, especially going into the playoffs, the Golden Knights could make another deep postseason run with roster that includes Jack Eichel and Mitch Marner.

stories.headline: What we learned: Selfless Lions maul Crows to leave Hawks shaking in their boots
stories.summary: From 53-point losers to 53-point winners, nobody rebounds like Brisbane. The three-peat is firmly on track.
stories.body:
GABBA -- Brisbane thrashed Adelaide on Saturday evening to book a fifth consecutive AFL preliminary final berth and send a major warning to the league's remaining finalists that its three-peat is firmly on track.

The Lions rebounded in style from last week's humbling defeat in Sydney and will now face Hawthorn at the MCG for a place in yet another Grand Final.

Here are three things we learned from the game:

The Lions are just two wins away from a magical dynasty ... and who would bet against them?
No team knows how to shake off a difficult loss quite like Brisbane. The Lions couldn't have played worse if they tried in last week's 53-point qualifying final defeat to Sydney at the SCG. The Swans, fresh off one of the most difficult fortnights in club history, caught lightning in a bottle and had the reigning champs rattled in the opening minutes. All of Brisbane's prime movers were well below their best and at no stage did they look like working their way into the contest. But that was last week.

Seven days later the Lions side showed why they are the back-to-back reigning premiers, bouncing back in emphatic style to record a 53-point win of their own, a crushing defeat of Adelaide to once again book a place in the last four. Brisbane flew out the gate, enjoyed the first 10 inside 50s of the night and put five goals on the Crows in just seven minutes and 13 seconds. By quarter-time it was 42-15 -- the Lions' highest score in the first quarter of a final since 1999.

So many of Brisbane's stars bounced back from their poor outings the week before. Charlie Cameron was electric with five goals. Zac Bailey, fresh from an eight-year contract extension during the week, kicked three goals from his 23 disposals. Kai Lohmann and Cam Rayner provided headaches in the front half all night. Will Ashcroft returned to finals Will Ashcroft (more on him later).

The ability to immediately respond has been an enviable trait of Brisbane over the past 12 months. Last year, the Lions were also humbled in a road qualifying final. They then won their next three finals to lift the premiership cup. In fact, since 2022 this club is now 11-2 in win-or-go-home finals.

Even this year the Lions have been quick to make amends for their most inexplicable losses. A 44-point defeat to the Swans in Round 1 was followed by a 33-point win against the Saints. The 76-point loss to the Blues late in the season was followed by a 67-point crushing of the Hawks. Even the rough three-game stretch midyear that had the footy world questioning their hunger was followed by wins in 10 of their final 11 home-and-away games.

The Lions will now travel to the MCG to battle Hawthorn for a place in a fourth consecutive Grand Final. Just two wins separate this resilient club from a stunning three-peat, are you brave enough to tip against them?

Despite the reports and the blowout, Matthew Nicks should remain safe in his role
Adelaide's finals road came to an abrupt end on Saturday evening in Brisbane. It's a loss that will no doubt sting for some time, but there's certainly no shame in falling to the back-to-back reigning champs on their home deck, right?

The Lions were clearly the better side on the night but the difference really was the burst in the opening minutes and another similarly scary attacking onslaught midway through the second term.

Perhaps Adelaide threw its biggest punch last week against the Bulldogs after rumours began circulating that coach Matthew Nicks could be out of a job should his side fail to win the home elimination final. That seemed wildly unfair at the time and even more ridiculous now they've taken it up to Brisbane.

There should be absolutely zero pressure on Nicks. At the end of the day, a coach's job is to win games. Since the beginning of last year, Nicks has orchestrated 34 wins. Only Brisbane's Chris Fagan, Geelong's Chris Scott, and Fremantle's Justin Longmuir boast more in that time. The Crows have also only suffered two heavy defeats in that period (one of them was tonight). For reference, Brisbane's had seven. Anyone who has built that type of enviable record over a two-year period deserves, at the very least, the respect of not being made to feel as if they're on the coaching hotseat.

Why is there this unfair expectation that Nicks and the Crows should be achieving so much more than they are? Even the most one-eyed Adelaide supporter would concede this side's probably not a top three team on paper, so finishing the season in fifth or sixth place should hardly be considered a failed campaign. Until the Crows are heading backwards, Nicks should not have to worry about his job security.

Will Ashcroft really should have been an All-Australian over Murphy Reid
Two-time Norm Smith Medal winner Will Ashcroft etched the latest chapter into his remarkable finals legacy on Saturday evening, turning in a dominant display against the Crows to propel Brisbane into yet another preliminary final.

It continues a dominant season for the young Lion who is not only the bookmakers' favourite to be best on ground on Grand Final day for a third time in succession, but is widely tipped to finish in the top five of this year's Brownlow Medal count. And yet, amazingly, Ashcroft wasn't selected in last month's All-Australian team.

Second year Docker Murphy Reid was someone who did receive a blazer. So, let's compare the pair:

You be the judge of who deserved to be included in the prestigious team.

Both Reid and Ashcroft were unusually quiet in their side's qualifying final losses last week. Both lifted on semifinal weekend, but Ashcroft's 30 disposals, 13 score involvements, six clearances, seven inside 50s, seven marks, and almost 500 metres gained against the Crows were just about best on ground numbers. And while finals performances don't count towards the All-Australian team, Ashcroft's latest outing only highlights how much of a blunder it was not having him in the 2026 team.

stories.headline: Suns' Mark Williams to miss months after shoulder surgery
stories.summary: Phoenix Suns center Mark Williams had surgery Thursday to repair a torn labrum in his left shoulder and will miss several months.
stories.body:
Phoenix Suns center Mark Williams had surgery Thursday to repair a torn labrum in his left shoulder and will miss several months, the team announced Friday.

The 7-foot-1 Williams, 24, who signed a fully guaranteed three-year, $38 million deal to return to the Suns in free agency, suffered the injury during a recent offseason workout.

He was coming off the healthiest season of his four-year NBA career, appearing in 60 games after a previous high of 44. He averaged 11.7 points, 8.0 rebounds and 0.9 blocks in 23.6 minutes per game.

Williams arrived in Phoenix in a 2025 draft night deal from Charlotte, after the Hornets' first attempt to trade him was rescinded shortly at that year's trade deadline. Williams took over as the Suns' starting center and was part of a group that helped Phoenix beat preseason expectations in earning a playoff berth.

He has career averages of 12 points, 8.5 rebounds and one block per game.

Without Williams, the Suns will likely lean on Oso Ighodaro and Khaman Maluach to play the bulk of the minutes at center this season.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

stories.headline: Warriors moved to Eden Park for Knights showdown
stories.summary: The Warriors are set to break records for their biggest home crowd in a final with Eden Park the venue for the elimination final against Newcastle.
stories.body:
The Warriors will make history when they host their first NRL final at Eden Park after the governing body announced the venue for the club's elimination final.

The NRL confirmed the Warriors would play Newcastle at Eden Park next Sunday at 6.05pm (4.05pm AEST) in week two of the finals.

The Warriors' first preference is to play at Mt Smart Stadium where their support is through the roof.

Eden Park holds 50,000 people however and is a more modern stadium, compared to Mt Smart where a sold-out crowd of 26,131 created a cauldron-like atmosphere in the Warriors' 26-16 loss to the Dolphins in Saturday night's qualifying final.

The Warriors have hosted five finals in their history in Auckland, but all at Mt Smart.

The Warriors have injury concerns ahead of the clash with the Knights, who they beat 46-32 in Auckland in round 25.

They lost strike centre Leka Halasima in the warm-up to the Dolphins clash with the Tonga international clutching at his right leg.

"It was a hamstring in the warm-up, nothing related to what he's been having which was an ankle injury," coach Andrew Webster said.

"He just felt his hamstring in the first stride out and reported it straight away yeah, couldn't go.

"I don't know any more than that right now."

Halasima is set to miss the Newcastle clash amid fears that prop Jackson Ford's injury comeback will be short-lived.

Ford, on return after a 12-week pectoral tear layoff, limped off against the Dolphins with an ankle complaint.

"Not good," Webster said, when asked about the nature of the injury.

"We don't know much more."

The Warriors were never in full cry in attack against the Dolphins with five penalty goals edging them to a 16-8 lead, but also denying them the chance near the opposition tryline to perhaps put the game to bed.

"We didn't get the opportunity to get a flow in to our attack," Webster said.

"That's the negative side of taking the penalty goals. But to stretch the lead out to eight points, we had to do it. It's a no-brainer.

"The negative side is there, but the eight-point gap is what every team should take."

Webster said the Warriors were in a strong position when leading 12-8 at halftime, but were unable to contain Dolphins centre Herbie Farnworth in particular as their tackles failed to stick.

"We were trying so hard ... chasing contact and collision, and they were pinballing. We have to be more efficient next week."

stories.headline: Acuña homers for Braves, Mahle turns in another stellar outing in 12-2 rout of Phillies
stories.summary: — Ronald Acuña Jr. homered to spark an eight-run fourth inning and Tyler Mahle turned in another stellar outing to lead the Atlanta Braves to their second straight victory over the Philadelphia Phillies, 12-2 on Saturday night.
stories.body:
ATLANTA -- — Ronald Acuña Jr. homered to spark an eight-run fourth inning and Tyler Mahle turned in another stellar outing to lead the Atlanta Braves to their second straight victory over the Philadelphia Phillies, 12-2 on Saturday night.


The Braves had to rally three times in 11 innings to win the series opener between the two top NL East teams. This one was a lot easier.


Acuña hit a towering shot that barely cleared the wall in front of the Phillies bullpen off Brooks Raley (5-7), who took the loss for the second straight night. Acuña tacked on a run-scoring single to close out the big inning.


Philadelphia was one out from escaping the inning with no further damage. Ozzie Albies walked and Michael Harris II singled before the Phillies, going with a bullpen game after Jesús Luzardo was scratched with a tight shoulder, called in Grant Holman for his first big league appearance of the season.


Mauricio Dubón had a two-run single, Drake Baldwin brought in two more runs with a double off the wall, and some sloppy play by the Phillies led to five unearned runs in the fourth. Bryson Stott had a throwing error on a routine play that would've ended the inning, and another run scored on a wild pitch.


Mahle (5-10) has pitched brilliantly for the Braves since the journeyman was acquired ahead of the trade deadline. He surrendered only a first-inning homer to Bryce Harper over seven innings, improving to 3-1 with a a 1.25 ERA in seven starts with Atlanta.


He allowed just six hits with three strikeouts and no walks.


Harris added a three-run homer in the eighth off Phillies catcher Garrett Stubbs.


Up next
RHP Grant Holmes (9-5, 3.46) will try to give the Braves a sweep on the series when he takes the mound Sunday against Philadelphia RHP Andrew Painter (3-9, 5.71).

stories.headline: France tops host Germany to reach FIBA World Cup final
stories.summary: Gabby Williams had 22 points and five rebounds to lead France to the final of the women's FIBA World Cup with a win over host Germany.
stories.body:
BERLIN -- Gabby Williams led France to the final of the women's FIBA World Cup with an 86-64 win over host Germany on Saturday.

Williams scored 22 points and had five rebounds to put France in touching distance of the title after a dogged performance from the host, which refused to give up in front of a partisan crowd at Berlin Arena.

"A tricky game," France coach Jean-Aime Toupane said.

Janelle Salaun had a double-double with 14 points and 11 rebounds, while Marine Johannes, who contributed three 3-pointers among her 13 points, slowed the game down in the final quarter.

"It was really a fight tonight. I think we were ready for that," Johannes said.

It was the first semifinal appearance for both teams since the stage was introduced in 1986.

France will play Spain or the United States, the four-time defending champion and tournament favorite, in Sunday's final. Their semifinal was later Saturday.

There was an air of nervous anticipation around the arena before tipoff as Germany, already further than ever before in its second tournament appearance, would need another major upset to make the final. Germany coach Olaf Lange spoke of "German basketball's best day" after the quarterfinal win over European champion Belgium.

Germany rued 25 turnovers on an evening when French pressure took its toll.

"When you have 25 of them and 10, 12 in my personal opinion were unnecessary or careless, it's very, very difficult to stay in a game against France," Lange said.

Germany, which recovered impressively since losing its opening game to Spain by 30 points, kept France below 90 points for the first time in the tournament and can look forward to the possibility of a bronze medal on Sunday.

"It's our third back-to-back [game] this tournament, which is insane. Honestly, it's crazy in that kind of tournament, a World Cup, to have three back-to-backs," forward Leonie Fiebich said. "We know what to do. We had a really tough game in the first game. We turned around and played really well the next game. So that's our plan, and everything's positive from now on."

stories.headline: Cris Cyborg is still going strong as a force in women's P4P top 10
stories.summary: At age 41, PFL women's featherweight champion continues win streak to secure spot in ESPN P4P top 10.
stories.body:
Cris Cyborg is an MMA legend. Period. End of story.

Actually, the Cyborg story continues, even with her being 41 years old and having spent 21 years in the sport. A champion in an unprecedented five fight promotions, she has long been a fixture in the ESPN pound-for-pound women's rankings. And by posting her 30th career victory -- the most ever by a woman in MMA -- at PFL Tampa on Saturday to retain the women's featherweight championship, Cyborg solidified her hold on the No. 3 spot.

It wasn't easy, not like so many past Cyborg fights in which she aggressively bowled over opponents to score quick knockouts. Ketlen Vieira put up a fight, bloodying Cyborg's face and achieving controlling positions on the canvas several times. But Cyborg persevered, nearly doubling Vieira's strike output and earning a unanimous decision win. As a result, the ESPN voting panel kept her right where she was in the top three.

For the ESPN divisional MMA rankings, click here.

Note: Results are current; rankings are as of Aug. 26. To be eligible for the rankings, a fighter must have competed over the past 12 months or must have an upcoming fight booked. Fighters who have been dropped for inactivity can be reinstated only after they compete.

Women's pound-for-pound rankings

1. Valentina Shevchenko

UFC flyweight

Record: 26-4-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Zhang Weili, Nov. 15, 2025

Next: TBA

Shevchenko's dominance came under question in 2022 and 2023, when she went 1-1-1 in a trilogy with Alexa Grasso. Boy, does that feel like a long time ago now. Shevchenko has more than reasserted herself as the best flyweight in the world, and now she's established herself as the No. 1 woman in the world, period. It wasn't surprising that she beat Zhang, but it was surprising how easy she made it look. Shevchenko is out injured, however, so she has vacated her UFC title, which will be up for grabs when Natalia Silva meets Wang Cong on Oct. 3.

2. Zhang Weili

UFC flyweight / strawweight

Record: 26-4

Last: L (UD) vs. Valentina Shevchenko, Nov. 15, 2025

Next: TBA

It's hard to move up in weight, especially at the highest level. That sounds like it should be obvious, but Zhang had been dominant at 115 pounds for so long, some of us might have taken for granted how big of a challenge moving to 125 would be. UFC 322 was a bad night for Zhang, but she doesn't have many. And if she decides to stay at flyweight, it certainly seems reasonable to believe she'll fare better in the future.

3. Cris Cyborg

PFL featherweight champion

Record: 30-2, 1 NC

Last: W (UD) vs. Ketlen Vieira, Aug. 22

Next: TBA

It had been a while since Cyborg had fought an elite opponent in MMA until she met Larissa Pacheco in 2024. That was a legitimate matchup -- and many within the industry were predicting Cyborg's downfall. Instead, she took out the PFL's two-weight champion, upending all of Pacheco's momentum. One of the original pioneers of women's MMA is once again a champion after getting her second career submission at PFL Lyon in December. The PFL promoted her fight with Vieira as a retirement bout, but after her win Cyborg did not sound like someone who is done fighting.

4. Mackenzie Dern

UFC strawweight champion

Record: 17-5

Last: W (UD) vs. Gillian Robertson, Aug. 15

Next: TBA

Dern's rise to the 115-pound throne was truly a changing of the guard. She is the division's first first-time champion since 2019, because the previous three champs -- Zhang Weili, Carla Esparza and Rose Namajunas -- all were in their second reigns. Dern, nearly a decade into her MMA career after multiple jiu-jitsu world championships, has won four fights in a row, including a dominant performance against a fellow grappling-heavy fighter, Robertson, in her first title defense.

5. Natalia Silva

UFC flyweight

Previous ranking: Tied for 4

Record: 20-5-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Rose Namajunas, Jan. 24

Next: Oct. 3 vs. Wang Cong

Silva is looking every bit the part of a future UFC champion following a dominant display against Alexa Grasso at UFC 315 and a victory over Namajunas at UFC 324. Silva's stick-and-move style has frustrated even the highest level of opponent, and she's got youth on her side as she won't turn 30 until 2027. With an injured Valentina Shevchenko having vacated the title, Silva will fight Wang for the belt at UFC 332.

6. Manon Fiorot

UFC flyweight

Record: 13-2

Last: W (TKO1) vs. Jasmine Jasudavicius, Oct. 18, 2025

Next: Sept. 12 vs. Alexa Grasso

Fiorot has handled everyone the UFC has put in front of her -- except the champion, Valentina Shevchenko, who defeated the Frenchwoman at UFC 315 in May 2025. But Fiorot could earn another shot at the belt if she can get past Grasso, a former champion, at Noche UFC.

7. Dakota Ditcheva

PFL flyweight

Record: 16-0

Last: W (UD) vs. Denise Kielholtz, July 31

Next: TBA

Not only did Ditcheva win the PFL's flyweight season in 2024, but she did so in spectacular fashion -- a TKO finish over Taila Santos, who once challenged for a UFC title. Ditcheva fought only once in 2025, dominating Sumiko Inaba in the co-main event of the first PFL Champions Series card in Cape Town, South Africa. She then spent over a year on the sideline, healing injuries to both hands, before returning at PFL New York with a dominant win over Kielholtz.

8. Erin Blanchfield

UFC flyweight

Record: 14-2

Last: W (Sub2) vs. Tracy Cortez, Nov. 15, 2025

Next: Oct. 17 vs. Jasmine Jasudavicius

Her rise toward the top of the division was derailed by a March 2024 loss to Manon Fiorot, but Blanchfield bounced back with two straight wins, including one over two-time former strawweight champion Rose Namajunas in November 2024. If she wins her October bout with Jasudavicius, a fellow top-10 flyweight contender, Blanchfield would inch ever closer to a title shot.

9. Tatiana Suarez

UFC strawweight

Record: 12-1

Last: W (Sub2) vs. Loopy Godínez, April 11

Next: TBA

If Suarez is still feeling the effects of last year's humbling defeat to Zhang Weili in a title challenge, she certainly didn't show it at UFC 327, overcoming early adversity to thrash Godinez, a fellow top-10 strawweight. Suarez is going to be a tough out for anyone at 115 pounds.

10. Alexa Grasso

UFC flyweight

Record: 17-5-1

Last: W (KO) vs. Maycee Barber, March 28

Next: Sept. 12 vs. Manon Fiorot

Grasso went nearly three years without winning a fight, but her 2023 win right before the skid was a huge one, a submission of Valentina Shevchenko for the UFC title. What followed were two more fights with Shevchenko -- a draw, then a loss -- and then a loss to Natalia Silva. That made the fight with Barber a must-win, and Grasso came through explosively. Next up is Fiorot, a fellow title contender.

Other fighter receiving votes: Virna Jandiroba.

How our panel voted
Brett Okamoto: 1. Valentina Shevchenko; 2. Zhang Weili; 3. Mackenzie Dern; 4. Cris Cyborg; 5. Manon Fiorot; 6. Dakota Ditcheva; 7. Natalia Silva; 8. Erin Blanchfield; 9. Tatiana Suarez; 10. Virna Jandiroba.

Carlos Contreras Legaspi: 1. Shevchenko; 2. Cyborg; 3. Zhang; 4. Ditcheva; 5. Dern; 6. Silva; 7. Alexa Grasso; 8. Suarez; 9. Fiorot; 10. Blanchfield.

Andrew Davis: 1. Shevchenko; 2. Zhang; 3. Cyborg; 4. Dern; 5. Silva; 6. Fiorot; 7. Blanchfield; 8. Ditcheva; 9. Suarez; 10. Jandiroba.

Dre Waters: 1. Shevchenko; 2. Zhang; 3. Cyborg; 4. Silva; 5. Dern; 6. Fiorot; 7. Ditcheva; 8. Blanchfield; 9. Suarez; 10. Grasso.

Jeff Wagenheim: 1. Shevchenko; 2. Zhang; 3. Cyborg; 4. Fiorot; 5. Silva; 6. Dern; 7. Blanchfield; 8. Suarez; 9. Ditcheva; 10. Grasso.

Men's pound-for-pound rankings

1. Islam Makhachev

UFC welterweight champion

Record: 29-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Ian Machado Garry, Aug. 15

Next: TBA

Makhachev vacated the UFC lightweight championship to go for a second title at welterweight. By winning that belt last November with a thrashing of Jack Della Maddalena, Makhachev staked his place among MMA's greatest -- not just in today's sport but of all time. His win over Machado Garry at UFC 330 was his 17th straight, breaking the UFC record for consecutive wins. Makhachev is piling up unprecedented achievements.

2. Petr Yan

UFC bantamweight champion

Record: 20-5

Last: W (UD) vs. Merab Dvalishvili, Dec. 6, 2025

Next: Oct. 24 vs. Dvalishvili

What a return to the top it's been for Yan. He began his career with 15 consecutive wins before going on a 1-4 run from 2021 to 2023. That almost doesn't feel real now, after watching him reclaim his throne against Dvalishvili, who once handed him the worst loss of his career. Yan took a major detour, but this was the destination we felt he was capable of before the skid. He once again looks like one of the best fighters on the planet. He can prove it by beating Dvalishvili again.

3. Merab Dvalishvili

UFC bantamweight

Record: 21-5

Last: L (UD) vs. Petr Yan, Dec. 6, 2025

Next: Oct. 24 vs. Yan

Dvalishvili was on one of the most impressive runs through the UFC's bantamweight division ever. Not only did he defeat Sean O'Malley for the second time in nine months at UFC 316, but he showcased a new part of his game, finishing O'Malley with a guillotine. Starting in August 2022, Dvalishvili beat José Aldo, Yan, Henry Cejudo, O'Malley (twice), Umar Nurmagomedov and Cory Sandhagen. But at UFC 323, in an attempt to become the first champion in UFC history to successfully defend a title four times in a calendar year, Dvalishvili lost a rematch with Yan. They will fight for a third time at UFC 333.

4. Tom Aspinall

UFC heavyweight champion

Record: 15-3, 1 NC

Last: NC1 vs. Ciryl Gane, Oct. 25, 2025

Next: TBA

You can make a case that Aspinall is the most dynamic, skillful, talented heavyweight the sport has seen. He is dominating opponents in a way that is unmatched. No one can last a round with him. He had hoped to prove his supremacy against Jon Jones, but Jones opted to retire, elevating Aspinall from interim champion. His first defense of the undisputed belt ended anticlimactically, as an eye poke resulted in his UFC 321 fight with Gane being declared a no-contest. Where does Aspinall go from here?

5. Ilia Topuria

UFC lightweight

Record: 17-1

Last: L (TKO4) vs. Justin Gaethje, June 14

Next: TBA

Topuria was an undefeated two-division champion when he ran into Gaethje at UFC Freedom 250 and was brutalized in a stoppage loss. How will that affect the immediate future of Topuria? His knockout wins over two of the greatest featherweights, Alexander Volkanovski and Max Holloway, gave him an intimidating aura. Can the former champion get that back?

6. Justin Gaethje

UFC lightweight champion

Record: 28-5

Last: W (TKO4) vs. Ilia Topuria, June 14

Next: TBA

Gaethje has spent his 15-year career thrilling MMA fans, but before the title bout on the White House lawn, all he had to show for it -- aside from 15 bonus checks in 15 UFC appearances -- were two missed opportunities to be an undisputed champion. His fourth-round TKO of Topuria got Gaethje over the hump. It was a resilient performance in a back-and-forth battle that is a prime candidate for fight of the year. More important for Gaethje: At age 37, he is finally sitting at the top of the mountain.

7. Alexander Volkanovski

UFC featherweight champion

Record: 28-4

Last: W (UD) vs. Diego Lopes, Jan. 31

Next: Oct. 24 vs. Movsar Evloev

It felt as if the sport had started to write Volkanovski's eulogy following his knockout loss to Ilia Topuria in February 2024. Volkanovski noticed and made a point of proving to everyone he still has plenty left by recapturing the featherweight belt at UFC 314, the first of two consecutive wins over Lopes. His age (37) will likely continue to be a prefight topic, which is fine because Volkanovski enjoys proving people wrong. Can he hand Evloev his first loss at UFC 333?

8. Alexandre Pantoja

UFC flyweight

Record: 30-6

Last: L (TKO1) vs. Joshua Van, Dec. 6, 2025

Next: Sept. 19 vs. Joshua Van

Pantoja became the UFC's unquestioned flyweight king by racking up four title defenses, including two in pay-per-view main events in 2024. He built his winning streak to eight in his UFC 317 win over Kai Kara-France, whom he had already defeated before, like other challengers. But he lost his belt in a gruesome way, injuring his elbow in the opening seconds of a UFC 323 fight with Van. Pantoja gets his rematch with Van at UFC 331.

9. Ciryl Gane

UFC heavyweight interim champion

Record: 14-2, 1 NC

Last: W (TKO2) vs. Alex Pereira, June 14

Next: TBA

Gane is unique in that he is the first -- and could very well go down as the only -- heavyweight to face the division's four biggest names in Francis Ngannou, Jon Jones, Tom Aspinall and Pereira. None of those four have fought each other, yet all four have have fought the Frenchman. Gane was 0-2 with a no-contest against that group before he knocked out Pereira in the second round of their interim title fight. Gane was heralded as the future of the generation when he broke onto the scene, but endured growing pains in losses to Ngannou and Jones. He looks formidable now, and no one will be counting him out if he faces Aspinall in a title unification bout.

10. Alex Pereira

UFC heavyweight / light heavyweight

Record: 13-4

Last: L (TKO2) vs. Ciryl Gane, June 14

Next: TBA

He was on the verge of making history when the opportunity fell apart. Pereira was a UFC champion at middleweight, then light heavyweight, but his unprecedented pursuit of a belt in a third weight class did not go well for the Brazilian, who lost an interim heavyweight title fight to Gane on the White House card. At 39 years old, Pereira does not have much time left to recapture the magic.

Other fighters receiving votes: Joshua Van and Arman Tsarukyan.

How our panel voted
Brett Okamoto: 1. Islam Makhachev; 2. Petr Yan; 3. Merab Dvalishvili; 4. Ilia Topuria; 5. Alexander Volkanovski; 6. Ciryl Gane; 7. Tom Aspinall; 8. Arman Tsarukyan; 9. Alex Pereira; 10. Alexandre Pantoja.

Carlos Contreras Legaspi: 1. Makhachev; 2. Volkanovski; 3. Justin Gaethje; 4. Topuria; 5. Pereira; 6. Dvalishvili; 7. Gane; 8. Joshua Van; 9. Yan; 10. Pantoja.

Andrew Davis: 1. Makhachev; 2. Aspinall; 3. Yan; 4. Dvalishvili; 5. Pantoja; 6. Gaethje; 7. Topuria; 8. Volkanovski; 9. Gane; 10. Pereira.

Dre Waters: 1. Makhachev; 2. Aspinall; 3. Yan; 4. Dvalishvili; 5. Pantoja; 6. Gaethje; 7. Volkanovski; 8. Topuria; 9. Gane; 10. Van.

Jeff Wagenheim: 1. Makhachev; 2. Aspinall; 3. Pantoja; 4. Yan; 5. Gaethje; 6. Dvalishvili; 7. Topuria; 8. Gane; 9. Pereira; 10. Volkanovski.

stories.headline: Source: Jaguars, Parker Washington unlikely to agree to deal
stories.summary: The Jaguars and Parker Washington are unlikely to agree to a contract extension before the start of the season, a source told NFL Network.
stories.body:
The Jacksonville Jaguars and wide receiver Parker Washington are unlikely to agree to a contract extension before the start of the season, a source told NFL Network's Cameron Wolfe.

The Jaguars explored extensions for Washington in the same range as Michael Wilson's recent three-year, $75 million contract with the Arizona Cardinals, the source told Wolfe, but the sides still didn't have a deal as of Saturday night.

Washington, who is coming off a breakout 2025 season and is entering the final year of his rookie contract, is betting on himself in what will be a pivotal 2026.

Washington said this past Wednesday that he was focused on the 2026 season, regardless of the ongoing contract talks.

"To me, my job is to come out here and stay ready to go, just do my job, be the best receiver I can be and make plays for the team," Washington said, according to Jaguars.com. "I'm just focused on me, being the best teammate I can be and having fun out here.

"If we get it done, that's cool. If not, I'm going to go out Sunday and leave my best out there."

Washington, 24, had 58 receptions for 847 yards and five touchdowns -- all career highs -- in 2025. The former sixth-round draft selection also scored two touchdowns as a punt returner last season.

stories.headline: Arsenal's Gabriel 'eager' to take another Champions League final penalty: 'If it happens again, I'll be there'
stories.summary: Arsenal defender Gabriel Magalhães has said that he is "eager" for another chance to take a penalty in a Champions League final.
stories.body:
Arsenal defender Gabriel Magalhães has said told ESPN that he is "eager" for another chance to take a penalty in a Champions League final after the heartbreak of missing the crucial spot kick in last season's final against Paris Saint-Germain.

Following an earlier miss from Eberechi Eze in the shootout, Arsenal's hopes of winning their first European trophy rested on the shoulders of the Brazil defender who ultimately sent the ball over the crossbar to crown PSG champions for a second consecutive season.

Gabriel, a stalwart character of the Arsenal defence, told ESPN Brasil that if he was in a similar position again, he would take another penalty.

"I couldn't let a single missed penalty erase everything I'd achieved during the season," he said.

"So, I just thank God for the opportunity to have been there in that moment, it's part of the football.

"But I'm definitely eager for another chance, if it happens again, I'll be there, and if I have to take the penalty, I'll take it. So, that's it."

Arsenal were praised throughout last season's campaign for their solid defence, conceding just seven goals throughout their European campaign.

Gabriel thanked the fans for their continued support despite their European season ending on a sour note.

"But like I said, it's part of football. I'm here, and it's not the first time something like this has happened. So, as I said, if there's another penalty for me to take, I'll take it."

Despite the missed opportunity in the Champions League final, Arsenal did end their 22-year wait for the Premier League title and look as though their form is continuing on into this campaign.

stories.headline: Kimi Antonelli jokes on opening stages of Spanish GP in Madrid: 'Driving like a grandmother'
stories.summary: Kimi Antonelli has said that taking on the brand-new Madring will be like driving like a Grandma in the opening stages of the Spanish Grand Prix on Sunday.
stories.body:
MADRID -- Kimi Antonelli has likened the challenge of the brand-new Madring to driving like a grandmother in the opening stages of Sunday's Spanish Grand Prix.

The Italian youngster was on provisional pole and was looking like the man to beat in qualifying before reigning world champion Lando Norris stunned him to the line by 0.011 seconds.

But the drivers have still been getting to grips with the track and heading into the weekend have referred to the the Madring to being "the most risky" on the Formula 1 calendar and "probably a car killer."

Antonelli joked that drivers will be driving like a grandmother and has warned that the race will be about managing the tyres.

"Yeah, probably it's going to be grandmother driving in the first 10 laps, but let's see," Antonelli said.

"We saw in the long run how steep the degradation can be, especially if you push too early, so let's see. We'll try to see in the moment, maybe tomorrow we're going to race and the degradation is going to be much lower, so we just need to see in the moment.

"Tomorrow is going to be a lot about managing the tyres and not degging [degradation] off, you know, so much as well. We don't really know how the hard tyre is, how resilient it is, so, you know, tomorrow we might have two stops, three stops.

"We'll see, but the key is, yeah, especially in that first stint is to try and manage as much, you know, without giving up too much time trying to manage the tyres."

- McLaren's Lando Norris pips Kimi Antonelli to take thrilling pole for Spanish Grand Prix

- Will Madring live up to reputation as F1 car killer? 'The most risky circuit of the calendar'

- Spanish Grand Prix: Everything you need to know about F1's brand-new Madring

Drivers and teams have no historic data to refer to when it comes to knowing how the car will perform this weekend, but one of the key talking points have been around how difficult it's going to be to overtake.

"I think it's going to be very difficult," Antonelli added. "In practice, I spent two laps behind the Williams trying to painfully get past, but just really difficult, especially because already the deg is quite big, and when you're behind, you start sliding more, and it just makes your life a bit tougher.

"The only thing you can do is try to put pressure on the car in front, try to make them do a mistake or make the deg a bit more, and then you try to play with strategy. But, yeah, especially when you have a very similar pace, it's difficult to make a move."

Antonelli is currently leading the world championship by 66 points adrift from his Mercedes teammate George Russell and will be aiming to take his seventh win of the season.

stories.headline: Dylan Larkin to attend Red Wings camp despite trade request
stories.summary: Longtime captain Dylan Larkin will be at Red Wings training camp despite requesting a trade this offseason. Though Larkin will be in attendance, the team said it will begin the season without a captain.
stories.body:
Longtime Red Wings captain Dylan Larkin will report to training camp in Detroit next week despite his summer trade request.

However the Red Wings announced that they will begin the season without a captain.

"Over the past couple of weeks, Red Wings leadership and I have had several in-depth discussions. I've appreciated those candid conversations, and I will be at training camp with my teammates," Larkin said in a statement. "When new leadership is in place, we'll talk further about the direction of the team. We will keep those conversations private, and I will keep my focus on the season ahead and on the guys in that room."

In July, shortly after Larkin's trade request became public, the Red Wings announced that Steve Yzerman would no longer be the team's general manager. Yzerman, a franchise legend and Hall of Famer, had been GM since 2019. Detroit entered a rebuild in that time and hasn't made the playoffs in 10 years.

In a statement, the Red Wings said they "look forward to seeing Dylan and his teammates at Little Caesars for the start of training camp," which begins Sept. 17.

"Any further discussions or decisions regarding this topic will be made once new hockey operations leadership is in place," the team said.

The Red Wings have hired a search firm, which has been conducting interviews for a new general manager.

Larkin, 30, grew up in nearby Waterford, Michigan, and played at the University of Michigan. He was selected by his hometown team in the first round of the 2014 NHL draft.

He debuted in the 2015-16 season for the Red Wings, and the team made the playoffs in his rookie season -- the final year of the franchise's NHL-record 25-year playoff streak. Detroit lost to Tampa Bay in five games in the first round and hasn't returned since.

Larkin was a key member of the 2026 U.S. men's Olympic team that won its first gold medal since 1980. He was especially important defensively and on special teams, part of a penalty killing unit that went a flawless 18-for-18 in Milan.

The Minnesota Wild -- led by Bill Guerin, also the general manager of Team USA -- have tried to acquire Larkin, according to sources. However the sides have been at a stalemate this summer, especially as Detroit's GM seat is vacant.

Larkin had been Detroit's captain since 2021. He ranks 10th in franchise history in both goals (276) and points (643).

The Red Wings' offseason has been defined by uncertainty. That led in part to the free agent departure of Patrick Kane, who returned to the Chicago Blackhawks. Another key piece of business that's unresolved: ascending star defenseman Simon Edvinsson is due for a contract extension.

stories.summary: Here are the top highlights from Brian Windhorst's "The Hoop Collective" podcast, from breaking news to the latest intel and reaction from around the NBA.
stories.body:
"The Hoop Collective" podcast, hosted by ESPN's Brian Windhorst, releases episodes every Monday, Wednesday and Friday during the NBA season and Tuesday and Friday during the offseason. Windhorst and his guests break down what's happening on and off the court, evaluating the trends you need to know and examining the latest news from across the NBA.

'The Hoop Collective' episodes

Sept. 11: Why the future of NBA Europe is uncertain

Brian is joined by Aris Barkas, the publishing director of Eurohoops, to discuss the future plans for the NBA in Europe, including if it's actually feasible, how it could possibly work out and the current state of European basketball.

Sept. 8: What history may tell us about Clippers' future + key signings in the West
Brian is joined by ESPN's Tim MacMahon to cover the latest fallout from the LA Clippers' punishment after the NBA announced its punishments for the franchise's off-the-court dealings with Kawhi Leonard. They discuss what league history could tell us about what's ahead for the Clippers and how LA got into this situation. They then close on key deals in the West, including Ben Simmons signing with the Sacramento Kings and Amen Thompson's extension with the Houston Rockets.

Topics:

0:27: Updates on the fallout from Clippers' punishment

6:37: Past may be an indicator of the future in LA

Windhorst on the league's reaction to the Clippers' punishment: "I think Steve Balmer had support of his peers in this, even though these was pretty severe accusations.

"I'm not saying everybody again, but I think people wanted to believe him, his peers. I'm not talking about the other GMs. I'm not talking about the agents. ...

"So the word that was said to me by a very influential person was that the other owners, some of the other owners were aghast when they read this report. That was the word that was used to me, aghast. And regardless of what Steve says, the support that he had is no longer there."

Windhorst on the Clippers' best course of action now: "When the Wolves were found guilty, Glen Taylor said words that were not, "I'm guilty." Kevin McHale, who was the vice president of basketball operations, said, 'I didn't even know this existed.' You know, he pled ignorance.

"[Then] They thought about it. They ended up negotiating with the league office and they pled guilty. And two days after basically they raised the white flag in December, David Stern gave him back a pick and a year later he gave him back the second pick. Now he gave them back -- he took away five years of picks [previously] -- he gave them back Year 3 at first and then Year 5. It wasn't like he gave him back immediately. But I think the Clippers should study that."

MacMahon on why Houston extended Thompson now: "I've been telling you for a while just how much the Rockets value Thompson. If there's one untradeable player on the roster, it is him.

"According to their metrics, they think he's one of the top 10 -- and I might be inflating that number -- most valuable players in the league. Now, we can argue and we can debate and you can say that's ridiculous. I'm just telling you the way that they view him. And so for them to get a player they value that much on this deal is great value for them.

"And for Amen Thompson, $208 million fully guaranteed and there's no options either way in the deal, he's set for life. He wants to be in Houston. He's going to be in Houston."

Sept. 3: EMERGENCY POD: NBA announces Clippers' punishments after Kawhi probe
Brian is joined by ESPN's Tim MacMahon to react to the hefty punishments handed down to the LA Clippers by the NBA after the investigation into Kawhi Leonard's off-court dealings. They break down what this means for the future of the Clippers, if the punishment makes sense and if this will impact Leonard's pending trade to the Toronto Raptors.

Topics:

1:25: NBA punishes Clippers after Kawhi probe

7:04 :The Clippers' argument against the NBA in this

10:36: What sticks out about the NBA's findings

16:47: What comes next for the Clippers?

30:21: How will this punishment impact Kawhi?

32:56: Who was most impacted by this punishment?

43:56: Final thoughts on this punishment decision

MacMahon on why the penalty was so large for the Clippers: "The simple fact of the matter is this ain't the first time Steve Balmer's pulled this shady stuff. That did not help his case.

"They gave him a little slap on the wrist for the DeAndre Jordan stuff in 2015. $250,000 fine. It was 'Oh, whoops. We didn't know.' And then, there's the investigation for the Kawhi signing because, guess what? It's not like Uncle Dennis only asked the Clippers for a whole bunch of under-the-table stuff. He was asking everybody for under-the-table stuff. 'Oh, geez. You know, we were asked, but we didn't, you know, didn't give him anything' and and now this. So, in a way they're three-time losers."

Windhorst on the Clippers' best course of action following the ruling: "If they could get an agreement, if they could plead guilty, get an agreement and and say, 'We're not going to challenge any of these penalties.' And they get an agreement that there'll be no further penalties -- basically, they'll say that these five first-round picks are all-encompassing, they cover everything. It's a blanket agreement and [then] they keep their nose clean, and they do the Kawhi trade, they might be able to come out of this without four broken limbs. They may be able to come out of this with less damage."

MacMahon on one of the winners of the investigation: "I do think Adam Silver in a way is a winner of this because straight up, he had been soft on crime as the commissioner since, ironically, he booted the previous Clippers owner, which was completely different circumstances."

Sept. 1: How Steph Curry can decide Warriors' future and major questions for Pistons
Brian is joined by ESPN's Tim MacMahon and Anthony Slater to discuss Stephen Curry's future with the Golden State Warriors, including how a potential extension could determine the franchise's outlook. They then move on to the Jalen Duren-Detroit Pistons situation, as his restricted free agency continues. Will this cause major issues for the Pistons' season? Slater on the potential Curry extension in Golden State and why he could wait: "One of the things in discussions I've been having with people is this idea of, let's say he's like, '[Taking less money for the team is] something I'd think about.' I would be surprised if he locked into a number now because, as you just saw with Draymond Green, the Warriors and their legendary figures are willing to trust each other in business.

"Draymond Green willingly gave up $27 million and went into unrestricted free agency where he couldn't have got $27 million back, [but] under the understanding if business didn't work out, he would get that money back. If you're Steph, you say, 'OK, you know what? I'll give y'all a crack at going and trying to find some stuff, but if you don't, at the end of the day, if I come back and say, give me the full max, I get the full max.'

"So, to answer your question, he doesn't have to necessarily lock into it now because they can't really execute [upgrading the roster]. Even if they could say, 'Hey, here's a theory of what we could do. Here's another theory of what we could do,' he could just say, 'All right, well, I'll hold off for now and see if you can do it, but at the end of the day, if I want the max, give me the max.'"

MacMahon on the Duren-Detroit situation: "He just averaged 19 [points] and 11 [rebounds]. He's a big physical force with some skill. I've talked to just executives from other teams around the league just kind of taking people's temperature and a lot of what I got is like, 'I can definitely see both sides of this,' because for the Pistons this is not an anti-Jalen Duren thing. This is a, 'We want to keep this core together.' By the way, they're also in the process of attempting to negotiate an extension with Ausar Thompson."

MacMahon on the Wembanyama-Jokic rivalry: "As much as Denver's summer was frankly a disaster, you can't just dismiss the Nuggets.

stories.headline: What We Learned: Sharks rediscover their bite; Trindall unlocks Hynes
stories.summary: Braydon Trindall allowed Nicho Hynes to play his best and the Sharks reaped the rewards, while the Cowboys season is over. Here's what we learned from the game.
stories.body:
Cronulla have kept their premiership hopes alive with a 26-16 elimination-final victory over North Queensland at Allianz Stadium.

The Sharks scored five tries in an encouraging attacking display, with Sione Katoa crossing twice before Nicho Hynes produced the defining moment to establish an unassailable lead.

Cronulla will now face the loser of Sunday's qualifying final between Penrith and the Sydney Roosters, while North Queensland's season is over.

Here are three things we learned from the game:

The Sharks thrive on confidence

Cronulla reminded us that confidence remains their greatest asset. When the tide turns in their direction, the fire is quickly lit -- and few teams can extinguish it.

Sione Katoa's intercept try was the perfect example.

The winger read Scott Drinkwater's pass, plucked the ball out of the air and raced 60 metres to restore Cronulla's lead. After Katoa crossed again shortly after halftime, the Sharks began playing with greater speed, freedom and ambition.

They nearly travelled the length of the field to score again immediately after Katoa's second, with the movement ultimately forcing a Cowboys error and earning Cronulla a scrum.

A similar surge followed Will Kennedy's try in the 60th minute. The Sharks again swept upfield before Hynes produced a piece of individual brilliance, dummying his way through the defensive line and crossing to push the margin out to 14 points.

It was the type of attacking football Cronulla are capable of when their confidence is flowing. Players support through the middle, passes stick and Hynes becomes increasingly willing to challenge the defensive line.

The concern for Craig Fitzgibbon's men is what happens when momentum is not behind them.

Whether their next opponent is Penrith or the Roosters, Cronulla are unlikely to be afforded the same opportunities to build confidence through repeat attacking movements. Both sides will attempt to slow the Sharks down and deny them the momentum that fuelled Saturday night's victory.

Cronulla showed how dangerous they can be once the fire is burning. The next challenge is learning how to light it themselves when a game is not naturally flowing their way.

Trindall's return unlocks Hynes

Nicho Hynes was back to his dangerous best on Saturday night, which should come as little surprise with Braydon Trindall restored alongside him.

Hynes acknowledged earlier in the week that Trindall performs much of Cronulla's traditional halfback work despite wearing the No. 6 jersey. That dynamic was evident against the Cowboys.

Trindall assumed greater control of Cronulla's shape and kicking game, allowing Hynes to pick his moments and play with freedom as a running threat.

The Dally M medallist ran the ball 15 times for more than 120 metres, broke five tackles and scored a sensational solo try. Receiving the ball close to the Cowboys' line, Hynes shaped to pass before stepping through the defence and accelerating into open space.

It was a decisive play from a player who has endured no shortage of scrutiny over his performances in big games.

Trindall's value to Cronulla extends beyond his own statistics. His presence gives the Sharks greater direction and reduces the burden on Hynes to organise every attacking set, kick long and then manufacture the decisive play.

Hynes is at his most dangerous when he can survey the defence and choose when to inject himself. With Trindall steering the side, Cronulla's highest-paid player can concentrate on becoming its most damaging one.

Drinkwater remains the ultimate high-risk, high-reward player

Scott Drinkwater was once again at his rocks-and-diamonds best, producing two try assists and four line-break assists while also committing four errors.

It can certainly be argued that the Cowboys would not have remained in the contest without him. Drinkwater directly created two of North Queensland's three tries and converted both, playing a role in 12 of their 16 points.

His sweeping cut-out pass to create the Cowboys' opening try was Drinkwater at his creative best: daring, instinctive and capable of seeing an opportunity that few other players would attempt.

But the same appetite for risk also produced costly moments.

His intercept pass gifted Katoa a 60-metre try at a crucial stage of the first half, while his handling and decision-making errors repeatedly halted North Queensland's momentum.

That contrast has always defined Drinkwater's game. He can manufacture points from nothing, but his determination to find the decisive play can occasionally hand momentum to the opposition.

It is his X factor that prompted St George Illawarra to sign him on a multiyear deal from 2027. The Dragons are betting that his creativity can transform their attack, while accepting the volatility that comes with it.

Saturday night provided the complete Drinkwater experience: breathtaking creativity, costly mistakes and a willingness to continue chasing the match regardless of what had happened on the previous play.

For North Queensland, however, the rewards were not quite enough to outweigh the risks.
